The proposed KBQA framework has these components:

- **Entity linker:** It takes an existing entity linker to produce the top-K linked entities for a question [3].
- **Relation detection model (HR-BiLSTM):** This model plays a key role in the process [4]. The end-task results refer to it as HR-BiLSTM [1][2].
- **Entity re-ranking:** Entity candidates are re-ranked according to whether they connect to high-confidence relations detected from the raw question text [4].
- **Core relation (chain) detection:** The core relation chains are found for each topic entity from a much smaller candidate set after re-ranking [4].
- **Constraint detection (optional):** This step is used when a question cannot be answered by single relations [4]. It is based on text matching and works like entity linking on a KB sub-graph [5]. It has two steps:
  - Sub-graph generation [5].
  - Entity linking on the sub-graph nodes, which uses the maximum overlapping character sequence between question n-grams and entity names [5].

The authors say the system takes minimal effort beyond training the relation detection model, which makes it easy to build [3].

The system must capture the morphosyntactic properties of a word from its context and map them to the correct surface form for the lemma [1].

The excerpts do not define a node outright, but they suggest that nodes are states (countries). The network combines two layers, one built from states' voting behavior and one from the speeches they make [2]. The approach does not require states to be similar on both dimensions [1]. In the speech layer, nodes are linked by text similarity [5]. Some nodes are "extraneous" ones added so that the nodes line up across the two layers [1].

No. The model has five independent decoders, one per image in the sequence [2]. Because each decoder is independent, each one learns a specific language model for its position. For example, the first decoder learns the opening sentences of the story and the last decoder learns the closing sentences [2]. The conclusions also say that having an independent decoder per position let the storyteller build more specific language models [3].

What the decoders share is their starting information. All of them use the encoder's last hidden state as their first hidden state, and each takes its corresponding image embedding as its first input [2][4].

The following features are extracted from tweets:

- **Emotion**: a vector built from word occurrences of 15 emotion types, drawn from two lexicons: NRC (eight Plutchik emotions) and SentiSense (categories not present in NRC) [1].
- **Sentiment**: positive and negative classes, extracted with EffectWordNet, SenticNet, NRC, and subj_lexicon [2].
- **Morality**: based on moral foundation theory, with 10 categories (care, harm, fairness, cheating, loyalty, betrayal, authority, subversion, sanctity, degradation) [2].
- **Style**: counts of question marks, exclamation marks, consecutive characters and letters, links, hashtags, and user mentions, plus the uppercase ratio and tweet length [2].
- **Word embeddings**: Glove-840B-300d embeddings of the tweet's words, averaged to give the tweet representation [2].

Ablation tests show that most of the performance gains come from word embeddings, style, and morality features [4].

Excerpts do not give an explicit layer count, but they describe three main layers. These are an LSTM recurrent layer [1], an attention layer with dropout [3], and a softmax output layer [3]. The size of the LSTM layer is a tuned hyperparameter (16, 32 or 64) [2].

The paper uses two datasets: the AMR Bank and the CNN-Dailymail corpus [1].

- **AMR Bank:** Only its proxy report section is used, because it is the only relevant part: it contains gold-standard (human-generated) AMR graphs for news articles, along with the summaries [1]. The training and test sets contain 298 and 33 summary-document pairs respectively [1].
- **CNN-Dailymail:** This corpus has around 300k document-summary pairs, and the stories average 39 sentences [2]. The authors use the non-anonymized version, which is more suitable for AMR parsing [2]. It has no gold-standard AMR graphs, so automatic parsers are used to obtain them [2].

The paper does not focus on one narrow kind of offensive content. It targets several kinds at once, modeling the task hierarchically to identify the type and the target of offensive messages [4]. This contrasts with earlier work that detected very specific types, such as hate speech, cyberbullying or cyber-aggression [4].

Prior work covered abusive language, (cyber-)aggression, (cyber-)bullying, toxic comments, hate speech and offensive language [1]. One earlier study on German tweets also split offensive tweets into profanity, insult and abuse [5].

The syntactic features obtained automatically on downstream task data are shallow syntactic features, specifically chunk information. The task training and test data are automatically chunked [1]. The chunk boundary information is then passed into the task model through BIOUL encoding of the labels [1]. Randomly initialized chunk label embeddings are added to the task-specific input encoders [1]. This approach needs only a chunker [1].

The authors give these examples:

- **General case:** A message can look harmless by itself but be seen as abusive once previous threads are considered, and the reverse can also happen [4]. This makes detection laborious even for human annotators and makes it hard to build a large, reliable dataset [4].

- **Bus example:** Tweet (2), "I hate it when I'm trying to board a bus and there's already an as**ole on it," is labeled abusive because of its vulgar language [1]. Its context tweet (1), about hating when someone with a wheelchair gets on the bus, helps show the user's intention [1].

- **Syria example:** Tweet (4), "Who the HELL is 'LIKE' ING this post? Sick people....", is abusive [2]. Its context tweet (3), "Survivors of #Syria Gas Attack Recount 'a Cruel Scene'," is important for identifying the target of the malice [1][2].

The two neural embedding models, both based on the skip-gram model, are:

1. **Concept Raw Context model (CRC)**, which uses concept mentions in a large-scale knowledge base to jointly learn embeddings of both words and concepts [1].
2. **Concept-Concept Context model (3C)**, which learns concept embeddings from their conceptual contexts, i.e., contexts containing only surrounding concepts [1].

Les extraits n'indiquent pas que les auteurs adoptent une architecture unique. Leur travail est une revue de la littérature sur les modèles de représentation de tweets, qu'ils organisent selon la fonction objectif optimisée [3]. Les modèles couvrent plusieurs architectures neuronales : moyenne de vecteurs de mots, modèles convolutionnels, modèles récurrents, etc. [2]. The model is evaluated on the WikiBio biography dataset introduced by lebret2016neural. It contains 700K {table, description} pairs and a vocabulary of about 400K words [2]. It pairs fact tables about people with their one-line biographical descriptions in English [4].

The authors also introduce two similar datasets, one in French and one in German [4]. Like the English dataset, they were built from Wikipedia infoboxes and the first sentence of the corresponding article [1]. They contain 170K and 50K examples, with vocabularies of 297K and 143K words, for French and German respectively [1]. All three datasets were split randomly into train (80%), test (10%) and validation (10%) sets [1].

Adversarial misspellings are a longstanding real-world problem, not just an academic one. Spammers keep misspelling words to evade spam detection while preserving the email's meaning [1]. Programmatic censorship has also led communities to adopt similar methods to communicate surreptitiously [1].

The adversary also has real leverage. Against word-piece or character-level models, each character-level add, drop, or swap produces a distinct input, which gives the adversary many options [2]. Standard defenses such as data augmentation and adversarial training offer only marginal benefits. For example, a BERT model's sentiment accuracy dropped from 90.3 to 64.1 under an adversarial 1-character swap, and adversarial training restored it only to 69.2 [5].

Diversity is calculated as the average dissimilarity of all pairs of tags in the list of recommended tags [2]. The calculation uses a distance function that gives the dissimilarity between two tags, and the result is averaged over the evaluated e-books [2]. To represent each tag, the previously trained Doc2Vec model extracts its latent representation [2]. The similarity of two tags is then computed with the Cosine similarity measure on their latent vectors [2].

The system uses TF-IDF features extracted from pre-processed pathology report text [4]. These features, together with training labels, are used to train different classification models to predict the primary diagnosis [4][5]. The approach does not rely on custom rule-based knowledge or domain-specific features [3].

TF-IDF weights are also used to identify keywords: all words in a report are sorted by TF-IDF weight, and the top 50 are taken as keywords [2]. These keywords are then grouped into topics using latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [2].

The qualitative metrics are the information extraction-oriented ones, designed by BIBREF10 [2]. There are three:

- **Relation Generation (RG):** estimates how well the system generates text containing factual (correct) records. It is measured by precision (RG-P%) and absolute number (RG-#) of unique extracted relations that also appear in the source table [5].
- **Content Selection (CS):** measures how well the generated document matches the gold document in terms of mentioned records. It is measured by precision (CS-P%) and recall (CS-R%) [5].
- **Content Ordering (CO):** analyzes how well the system orders the records discussed in the description. It is measured by the normalized Damerau-Levenshtein distance between the sequences of extracted records [5].

CS primarily targets the "what to say" aspect, CO targets the "how to say it" aspect, and RG targets both [4]. BLEU is the other, non-qualitative metric, measuring how literally close the generated descriptions are to the ground truth [2].

Multilingual BERT (M-Bert) reached a reasonable accuracy on x-stance [4]. The excerpts give no exact scores, only these qualitative findings:

- **Against baselines:** M-Bert performs consistently better than the majority class baselines in the cross-lingual setting [1]. Even zero-shot Italian is well above the target-wise majority baseline, though significantly below the supervised scores [1].
- **Cross-target:** Performance is worse than in the supervised setting, but M-Bert still easily surpasses the majority class baselines [1]. The cross-question score is slightly lower than the cross-topic score [1].
- **Supervised vs. transfer:** The supervised part of x-stance appears about as difficult as SemEval-2016 or MPCHI, on which BERT has previously been evaluated [4]. In the cross-lingual and cross-target settings, the mean score drops by 6–8 percentage points compared to the supervised setting [4].
- **Question language:** Cross-lingual performance clearly increases when all questions are given in English. The effect is negligible in most other settings [3].

The authors conclude that M-Bert has some capability for zero-shot transfer to unseen languages and targets, but that a performance gap remains [5].

They use three kinds of models:

- **Visual model:** it fine-tunes an Inception V3 model over visual renderings of documents [3]. Inception applies multiple convolution filters in parallel and concatenates the resulting features [5].
- **Textual model:** a hierarchical biLSTM [3]. It averages word representations to get a sentence representation, then feeds these into a biLSTM with a max-pooling layer to get a 512-dimensional document representation used to predict quality [1].
- **Joint model:** it combines the two [3]. It concatenates the 512-dimensional biLSTM representation with the 2,048-dimensional Inception representation, giving 2,560 dimensions [2].

The proposed model is compared with two groups of baselines.

1. Traditional models: TF-IDF features are fed into classic classifiers [2][4]. The Naïve Bayesian classifier (NB) scored highest among these [2].

2. Neural models: a Doc2vec model was pre-trained with Gensim, and its word embeddings were used to initialize the deep models, which were then fine-tuned [4]. Among them, the LSTM with self attention (LSTM-self) gave competitive results and was chosen as the base model [2].

The proposed model was also tested in other settings against that base model: Topic Only, ELMo Only, and ELMo+Topic [3]. The excerpts do not name the other classic classifiers or neural models.

The excerpts do not name a single state-of-the-art method. They do describe the recent neural grammar induction approaches that the proposed compound PCFG is compared against [4]:

- Two approaches learn tree structures through soft gating layers within neural language models [3].
- One approach combines recursive autoencoders with the inside-outside algorithm [3].
- One approach trains unsupervised recurrent neural network grammars with a structured inference network to induce latent trees [3].
- A further approach uses image captions to identify and ground constituents [3].

PRPN is also named as one of the compared models [2].

The neural PCFG and compound PCFG are described as strong grammar induction models. The compound PCFG outperforms the other models by an appreciable margin on both English and Chinese [5].

Based on the excerpts, accounts spreading fake news show these characteristics:

- **Verification:** 82 users in the sample spread fake news. Of these, 34 were verified and 48 unverified [1]. Fake news has a higher chance of coming from unverified accounts [1]. Among the 48 unverified accounts, 6 had been suspended by Twitter, 3 tried to imitate legitimate accounts of others, and 4 had been deleted [1].
- **Friends:** On average they have the same number of friends as accounts spreading viral tweets without fake news, but the distributions of friends differ in a statistically significant way [1].
- **Followers:** Their follower distribution is very different from that of accounts spreading viral tweets without fake news, and the differences are statistically significant [4]. On average they have fewer followers [2].
- **Friends/followers ratio:** They have, on average, a larger ratio of friends/followers, while accounts not spreading fake news are more evenly distributed [4].

The authors hypothesize that this ratio, together with the number of URLs in the tweet, could help single out fake news [2].

Word-like units are discovered with unsupervised term discovery (UTD). UTD works on raw acoustic features and uses segmental dynamic time warping (DTW) to identify and cluster repeating word-like units across speech [1]. The paper's abstract says the units are found without supervised ASR training [3].

The excerpts do not explain how the phoneme-like units are discovered. They refer only to an "AUD-based setting" and "automatically discovered phoneme-like units" [2].

The paper reports three simple baselines: NO-MOVE, RANDOM and JUMP [1]. They serve as lower bounds for the task [1]. The best of them was NO-MOVE, with 30.3% accuracy on single sentences and 0.3 on complete paragraphs [1]. By comparison, human paragraph accuracy reached above 80, which is the upper bound [1].

The excerpts give no numbers for RANDOM or JUMP.

Style transfer success was measured with human evaluators. They were shown pairs of an original and a translated sentence, and were asked whether the translated sentence sounded more formal, more informal, or neither compared with the original [5]. This was done on 100 sentences, 50 from OpenSubtitles and 50 from Europarl, each translated into the opposite style [5].

For each sentence pair, the three evaluators' answers were averaged. "More formal" counted as +1, "more informal" as -1, and "neither" as 0 [3]. The root mean square error (RMSE) was then computed between these averages and the desired value, +1 for aiming at more formal and -1 for more informal [3]. An RMSE of 0 means the style always moved in the right direction according to all evaluators, and 2 means it always moved in the wrong direction [3].

Sentences that all participants marked as unchanged were excluded, leaving 55 in English and 68 in Estonian to quantify style transfer quality [2].

The RMSE was 0.78 for English and 0.89 for Estonian. This indicates that style transfer generally goes in the right direction but is not very strong [4]. The direction was also counted directly. In English, 33 sentences went the right way, 7 the wrong way, and 15 showed no change. In Estonian the counts were 36, 10, and 22 [4].

Before the human evaluation, the authors also checked how often sentences changed when translated into different styles [1].

Excerpt [2] says the authors assume movie subtitles (OpenSubtitles) lean towards a more informal style, while parliament proceedings (Europarl) lean towards a more formal one [2]. Preliminary tests showed that JRC-Acquis and EMEA texts gave practically the same style as Europarl [2]. The method relies on parallel MT corpora in different styles and needs no parallel data between styles [3].

The excerpts do not define meta-knowledge precisely, but they describe it as follows:

- The meta network extracts the shared meta-knowledge across different compositional rules. It uses this to dynamically generate the context-specific compositional function [3].
- The shared meta TreeNN captures the general rules across different samples. This lets the model dynamically capture the diversity of semantic compositionality [1].
- In simple tasks such as text classification, the meta network integrates useful, task-specific semantic information into the generation of the compositional function. For example, one neuron is sensitive to emotional terms and signals that an informative phrase is coming [2].
- In more complicated tasks such as semantic matching, the meta network can capture some syntactic information. For example, one neuron monitors phrases built around a light verb [4].

The scorer is trained on a sensationalism dataset that the authors collected themselves [1]. Positive samples are headlines with many comments from popular online websites [1]. Negative samples are headlines generated by a sentence summarization model. The reasoning is that such a model, trained to preserve semantic meaning, loses the ability to sensationalize, so its headlines should be less sensational than the originals [1].

The resulting classifier reached 0.65 accuracy and 0.65 averaged F1 on the test set [2]. A baseline trained on headlines with few comments as negatives (a balanced corpus of 84k headlines) reached only 60% accuracy, so the proposed approach was chosen [2].

The excerpts do not state outright that the "best reported system" is Joshi et al. (2015), but this is the most reasonable reading. The paper's cognitive features improve F-score by 3.7% over the best reported system [2]. In the results, the 3.7% F-score improvement (MILR classifier) is stated relative to the baselines and to BIBREF3 [3]. The comparison for statistical significance is against the state-of-the-art system that uses textual sarcasm features alone, namely the linguistic features of joshi2015harnessing, run with an SVM classifier [1]. That feature set subsumes unigram features and features from other reported systems [4].
